title: The Test Plans model
summary: Test plans, suites, test cases, shared steps, parameters and configurations, and how they fit together.

lessons.title: Plans, suites and test cases
lessons.body:
Azure DevOps Test Plans organizes manual testing in three levels.

**Test plan.** The top container, usually tied to a sprint or a release, for example 'Release 3.2 test plan' or 'Sprint 14'. It has a name, dates (an area path and iteration path), and holds suites. A test plan is not a document. It is a living list of what will be tested and the results.

**Test suite.** A group of test cases inside a plan. There are three kinds.

| Suite type | How cases get in | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Static | You add them by hand | Smoke, regression, UAT, any custom grouping |
| Requirement-based | Created from a work item (a story or bug); the cases are linked to it | One suite per story, with traceability |
| Query-based | A work item query selects the test cases | Dynamic groups, for example all priority 1 cases for the notifications area |

Suites can be nested: a plan might have a parent static suite called 'Regression' with child suites per area. The plan structure is a tree you can reorganize.

**Test case.** A work item of type Test Case. It has a title, steps (action plus expected result), priority, area and iteration path, a state (Design, Ready, Closed), and links. Because it is a work item, you can query it, link it and report on it just like a story.

An important distinction: a **test case** is the definition and lives once. The same test case can appear in many suites and plans. The **test point** is that test case within a particular suite, with a configuration and a tester. Results attach to test points.

**Typical layout for the SOS release:**

```
Test plan: Release 3.2
  Suite: Smoke (static)            - 6 cases, run on every build
  Suite: Story 1234 SOS radius (requirement-based) - 9 cases
  Suite: Story 1240 SOS alert content (requirement-based) - 7 cases
  Suite: Regression: Scheduling (static) - 24 cases
  Suite: Open high-priority (query-based) - dynamic
  Suite: UAT (static) - 12 cases for customer staff
```

Add cases from the suite using a grid, or create new cases directly in the suite; both link them correctly. Keep titles consistent so people can search them.

Use the state field to mark readiness: cases in Design are draft, Ready are reviewed and executable. Many teams only run Ready cases.
keyPoints: Plan > suites > test cases; a plan is usually per sprint or release.
Three suite types: static, requirement-based, query-based.
A test case is a work item defined once and reusable across suites.
A test point is a test case in a suite with a configuration and tester; results attach to it.
Use case state (Design, Ready) to control what is executable.
lessons.interviewAngle: This lesson is your home ground. Describe how you structured plans: one per release or sprint, a smoke suite, requirement-based suites for traceability and a regression suite. Use exact terms. If the interviewer's tool is different, say the concepts transfer but you have used Azure DevOps Test Plans specifically.

exercises.prompt: Which suite type is created from a user story and keeps the cases linked to that story?
exercises.explanation: A requirement-based suite is built from a work item, so its cases are linked to that requirement for traceability.

exercises.prompt: Which suite type would you use to automatically gather every Priority 1 test case in an area?
exercises.explanation: A query-based suite pulls cases that match a work item query, so it updates as cases change.

exercises.prompt: What is the name for a test case within a specific suite, together with its configuration and tester, to which results are recorded?
exercises.explanation: Results are recorded against test points, not directly against the test case definition.

exercises.prompt: Design the test plan structure for a two-week sprint that delivers two SOS stories (radius selection and alert content). List the suites, their types and the purpose of each, and say how you would handle regression and UAT.
exercises.answer:
**Test plan:** Sprint 14 (iteration path Sprint 14).

- **Smoke** (static): 5 to 6 quick cases (sign in, send an SOS, view the request, cancel). Run on every new build to decide whether deeper testing is worthwhile.
- **Story: SOS radius selection** (requirement-based): cases derived from its acceptance criteria, linked to the story.
- **Story: SOS alert content** (requirement-based): cases for alert text, accept/decline, and the manager's count.
- **Regression: Notifications and Scheduling** (static, nested by area): existing cases for areas the changes could affect, selected by what the PRs touched.
- **High-priority open** (query-based, optional): all Priority 1 cases in the notifications area for quick executive checks.
- **UAT** (static): a short list of business-readable scenarios for the customer's staff, run near the end of the sprint or release.

Bugs found are linked to the story suite's story and the failing case.
rubric: Uses requirement-based suites for the stories
Includes a regression suite scoped to affected areas
Includes a UAT suite for customer staff

lessons.title: Shared steps, parameters and configurations
lessons.body:
These features reduce duplication and let one test case cover several situations.

**Shared steps.** A set of steps you use in many cases, saved once as a Shared Steps work item. The classic example is 'Sign in as pharmacy manager': username, password, click Sign in, expect the dashboard. Insert it into any test case. When the sign-in screen changes, you edit the shared steps in one place and every case is updated. Do not overuse it: a case that is just a list of shared steps is hard to read.

**Parameters.** A step can contain a placeholder written as `@radius`. Below the steps, a table of values defines each iteration:

| @radius | @expectedCount |
|---|---|
| 5 | 2 |
| 10 | 4 |
| 25 | 7 |

The case is then run once per row, and each iteration gets its own result. This replaces three near-identical cases with one, and the data is easy to review. Use parameters for data variations of the same flow, not for different logic.

**Shared parameters.** A parameter table saved once as its own work item and reused across several cases, so a change to the data set updates all of them. Useful for a standard list of test users or a common set of radius values. Cases can use a shared parameter set or their own local one.

**Configurations.** A configuration is an environment combination you test on, such as 'Chrome on Windows 11', 'Safari on iPhone' or 'Edge on Windows 10'. Each configuration has variables like browser and operating system. You assign configurations to a plan, suite or test case, and Test Plans creates a test point for each case-configuration pair. If a case has two configurations, there are two test points to execute. Be selective: testing every case on every configuration multiplies the work. Use risk to choose which suites need multiple configurations, for example the smoke suite on all browsers and regression on the main one only.

**Worked example.** One test case 'SOS radius limits alert recipients' using @radius and @expectedCount, starting with the shared steps 'Sign in as pharmacy manager'. It runs on Chrome and on Safari for mobile. That is three parameter rows times two configurations. Whether to run all six depends on the risk: the mobile layout matters most for pharmacists, so you would run all rows on mobile for the alert and one row on desktop.
keyPoints: Shared steps are reusable step blocks maintained in one place.
Parameters (@name) with a table of values run one case through several data sets.
Shared parameters let several cases reuse a data table.
Configurations (browser, OS) create separate test points; choose them by risk.
lessons.interviewAngle: Mention shared steps and parameters as how you kept a large suite maintainable. Give one real example, such as shared sign-in steps. Be honest about scale: you maintained a practical suite for a small product, not thousands of cases. Don't overstate your use of advanced features if you used only some of them.

exercises.prompt: Sign-in steps appear at the start of forty test cases and the sign-in page just changed. What feature makes this a one-place fix?
exercises.explanation: Shared steps are maintained once and inserted into many cases, so an edit updates all of them.

exercises.prompt: What symbol begins a parameter name inside a test step, such as @radius?
exercises.explanation: Parameters are written with a leading @ and values come from the table below the steps.

exercises.prompt: A test case has 3 parameter rows and is assigned 2 configurations. Roughly how many results will need recording if you run everything?
exercises.explanation: Each configuration produces a test point, and each point runs the parameter iterations, so 2 x 3 = 6.

exercises.prompt: Design one parameterized test case for the SOS radius rule (5, 10 or 25 miles). Give the title, the shared steps you would reuse, the parameter table with at least four rows including one invalid value, and the configurations you would use and why.
exercises.answer:
**Title:** SOS alert reaches only available pharmacists within the selected radius

**Shared steps (reused):** 'Sign in as pharmacy manager'; 'Open the SOS request form'.

**Steps:**
1. Select radius @radius and submit the request. Expected: confirmation 'SOS sent to @expectedCount pharmacists'.
2. Check the alert on a pharmacist inside the radius. Expected: alert shows pharmacy name and shift time.

**Parameters** (test data: pharmacists at 4, 9 and 20 miles):

| @radius | @expectedCount |
|---|---|
| 5 | 1 |
| 10 | 2 |
| 25 | 3 |
| 30 (invalid, attempted by editing the request) | Rejected, 0 alerts |

**Configurations:** Chrome on Windows (the main desktop browser) for the manager side, plus Safari on iPhone for the pharmacist's alert, because pharmacists mainly use phones. Other browsers only in the smoke suite.
rubric: Uses shared steps for sign-in or setup
Parameter table has valid values and an invalid one
Chooses configurations with a risk-based reason
